items.prompt: What makes a political move "black" rather than "white"?
choices: It is an attempt to influence a decision
It needs something kept hidden to succeed
It is carried out by someone with more power
items.explanation: White politics also tries to influence outcomes. The difference is that black politics needs something hidden or blurred to succeed.

items.prompt: Which description best fits credit-stealing?
choices: Presenting someone else's work as though it were yours
Praising a teammate more than they earned
Finishing a shared task later than planned
items.explanation: Credit-stealing moves the credit for real work from the person who did it to the person who presents it.

items.prompt: A teammate presents your model and says, "my colleague built this; here is what it shows." Is that black politics?
choices: Yes, any presenting of another's work is
Yes, because it makes the presenter look good
No, the builder is named openly
items.explanation: Naming the builder hides nothing. The presenter gains visibility without erasing who did the work.

items.prompt: Which question is a good transparency test?
choices: Will this help my manager notice my work?
Could I say this out loud to the room?
Is this a common habit here?
items.explanation: If explaining the move openly would make it fail or look worse, it probably depends on concealment.

items.prompt: What is scapegoating?
choices: Praising someone for work they did not do
Reporting a real mistake
Blaming someone for a failure not theirs
items.explanation: Scapegoating redirects blame for a shared or someone else's failure onto a person who was not responsible.

items.prompt: Which of these is white politics?
choices: Presenting a clear case openly
Letting people keep believing a rumor
Hinting a rival caused it
items.explanation: A clear, open case survives being stated aloud. The other two rely on hiding or blurring the truth.

items.prompt: What is a sensible reason to read a situation accurately before reacting?
choices: Accuracy makes colleagues like you more
Misreading in either direction carries a real cost
It lets you avoid every conversation
items.explanation: Treating an accident as an attack burns trust; treating a real pattern as an accident lets it repeat.

items.prompt: What does deniability mean in this unit?
choices: Refusing to answer a direct question
Declining a colleague's request for help
Holding an innocent excuse in reserve
items.explanation: Deniability is the built-in escape hatch: "I forgot" or "I did not mean it that way" after the credit has already moved.

items.prompt: After one readout, three colleagues are praised. A presents the team's model and names its two builders. B says "the approach I came up with" about a model a teammate built. C lobbies openly for a proposal and argues its merits in the meeting. Which is black politics, and why?
choices: A and B, because both gained visibility from shared work
Only C, because lobbying is an attempt to influence a decision
Only B, because the claim needs the true builder's role hidden
None of them, because each raised their own standing
items.explanation: A names the builders and C argues in the open; both survive being explained. B's gain exists only while the true builder stays out of view.
items.reference:
The transparency test
✅ White: could be said out loud to the room and still work
⛔ Black: only works while the real move stays hidden
🔍 Ask: what would change if everyone knew exactly what I did?
Why: the line is concealment at someone else's expense, not influence itself.
items.learnMore:
Influence is normal; concealment is the line

Every workplace runs on people trying to shape outcomes. Black politics is the subset that needs a hidden or blurred fact to succeed, such as who really built something, and that advances one person at another's expense. Naming it accurately matters because the right response to a genuine accident differs from the right response to a deliberate move.

Common mistake

Treating all visible ambition as political misconduct, or treating a real pattern as a harmless slip.
items.reflection: Think of a time you saw someone gain standing at work. Could they have described exactly what they did out loud, and would it have changed anything?

items.prompt: Two managers report the same true result in an all-hands. One names who produced it; the other leaves that out so people assume she did. What turns the second into black politics?
choices: It relies on the producer staying unclear
She framed the result in a favorable light
She presented it in front of the executives
She mentioned fewer names than the first
items.explanation: Positive framing and an audience are normal. The line is crossed because the benefit relies on a blurred fact about who did the work.

choices: Scapegoating
Sabotage
Manufactured urgency

items.prompt: Which tactic spreads unverified information while hiding where it came from?
choices: Manufactured urgency
Credit-stealing
Weaponized rumors
items.explanation: The hidden source is what makes a rumor a weapon: it hurts a reputation and cannot be traced back.

items.prompt: Falsely framing a decision as time-critical so nobody reviews it is called what?
choices: Weaponized rumors
Manufactured urgency
Plausible deniability
items.explanation: Manufactured urgency invents hurry to bypass normal scrutiny.

items.prompt: Quietly weakening someone's work while appearing supportive is called what?
choices: Scapegoating, blame placed afterwards
Credit-stealing, a claim in a meeting
Sabotage, often disguised as support
items.explanation: Sabotage often looks like help, which is why it usually takes a pattern to notice.

items.prompt: Which tactic is often visible in a single moment?
choices: Credit-stealing
Sabotage
Scapegoating
items.explanation: A specific claim in a specific meeting can be seen at once; the others tend to need a trail.

items.prompt: Which tactic usually requires tracing where information started?
choices: Scapegoating
Weaponized rumors
Credit-stealing
items.explanation: The source of a rumor is deliberately obscured, so tracing it is part of recognizing it.

items.prompt: Which deadline is NOT manufactured?
choices: "Decide today" with no reason given
An urgent flag from someone who gains
A contract expiry written into the signed terms
items.explanation: A real deadline has a stated, checkable cause. The others give no reason or come from someone who gains.

items.prompt: Is answering a rumor with a rumor of your own a good defense?
choices: Yes, it fairly evens out the score
No, it just trades one harm for another
Yes, provided your own rumor is accurate
items.explanation: Retaliating in kind trades one kind of damage for another and rarely fixes the original problem.

items.prompt: In a postmortem, a lead says the outage came from "the config change another engineer pushed." The lead had approved that change. Which tactic is this, and what would you gather first?
choices: Credit-stealing, plus the list of commit authors
Scapegoating, plus the record of who approved the change
Sabotage, plus the change's test results
Manufactured urgency, plus the deploy schedule
items.explanation: Blame is being placed on someone who did not decide. The approval trail shows who actually made the call.
items.reference:
Five tactics, five kinds of evidence
🎤 Credit-stealing: one specific claim in one specific moment
👉 Scapegoating: who actually decided, from a record
🧩 Sabotage: help that keeps weakening the work, over time
🗣️ Weaponized rumors: trace who said it first
⏱️ Manufactured urgency: what really happens if it waits
Why: each tactic damages trust differently, so each needs different evidence.
items.learnMore:
Name the mechanism, then match the evidence

Credit-stealing, scapegoating, sabotage, weaponized rumors and manufactured urgency all advance one person at another's expense, but they work differently. A claim made in a meeting can be noticed once. Blame, sabotage and rumors usually need a trail over time, and urgency needs the question of what actually happens if the date slips.

Common mistake

Using one response for all five, such as a public confrontation, when the evidence for each looks different.
items.reflection: Which of the five tactics would be hardest for you to spot in your own workplace, and what record would you need to see it?

Credit claims are always deliberate
Scapegoating never happens just one time
A sincere mistake looks identical once
items.explanation: Someone may sincerely misremember who decided. Claiming authorship over work you visibly built is much harder to explain innocently.

"I didn't mean to leave you out, honestly"
items.explanation: Deniability is the innocent-sounding excuse that stays available after the credit has already moved.

items.prompt: Why is one ambiguous incident hard to confront directly?
choices: Nobody else in the room noticed it
The person can offer an innocent excuse
Open confrontation is not allowed at work
items.explanation: With only one incident, "I did not mean to" is genuinely hard to disprove.

items.prompt: A public accusation after one ambiguous omission risks what?
choices: Proving that the omission was deliberate
Making the omission official policy
Looking petty if intent is not clear
items.explanation: If intent is not yet clear, the person raising it can appear to overreact even when the instinct is right.

items.prompt: After a private talk and then a repeat, the excuse "I did not know" does what?
choices: It no longer covers a repeating pattern
It becomes more believable
It is accepted without question
items.explanation: Once you have said something and it happens again, claiming ignorance no longer fits.

items.prompt: What is stronger evidence?
choices: One omission, since it happened first
Three omissions from the very same person
All of these carry equal evidential weight
items.explanation: A pattern from the same actor makes deniability on any single instance matter less.

items.prompt: Does deniability prove someone meant harm?
choices: Yes, an excuse is always a confession of guilt
Yes, whenever they sound calm
No, but it is a reason to build a record
items.explanation: It does not prove intent. It is a reason to document and respond proportionally.

items.prompt: Which response fits one ambiguous incident?
choices: Escalate it to the executive team
Raise it privately and start a record
Retaliate in the same way
items.explanation: A low-confrontation response protects both the relationship and your position.

items.prompt: "Here is the analysis," said with no names, is closest to what?
choices: An ambiguous omission
An explicit authorship claim
A proven pattern of theft
items.explanation: Without a claim of authorship, an oversight is a plausible reading. Wording matters.

items.prompt: You privately mention a missing credit, then the colleague omits it again at the next readout. Why is the "I did not know" excuse weaker now?
choices: Repeats are always proof of deliberate sabotage
The first excuse was effectively a confession
Managers must now act on it automatically
They can no longer plausibly claim ignorance
items.explanation: After the conversation, the omission happened with knowledge. That removes the cover deniability gave the first time.
items.reference:
What deniability does to your options
🤷 One ambiguous incident: an innocent excuse is plausible
📄 So the first response: raise it privately and start a record
🔁 After a talk and a repeat: "I did not know" no longer fits
Why: deniability weakens with repetition, so repeated evidence beats a single accusation.
items.learnMore:
Why a loud accusation is risky early

Most black-politics moves are built so the person can say "I did not mean it" afterward. Deniability does not prove harmful intent, but it makes a public accusation risky after only one incident, because you may look petty even if you are right. A calm record and a private question keep your options open, and a repeat after that question removes the excuse.

Common mistake

Treating every ambiguous moment as proof of a deliberate pattern.
items.reflection: Recall a time someone said "I did not mean it that way." What would have made you more, or less, willing to believe them?

All three are equally deniable since none names you
(b) is easiest to deny because it was spoken aloud
items.explanation: Passive omission has an innocent reading. An authorship claim is harder to explain. A repeat after a conversation removes ignorance as an excuse.

items.prompt: What is a good first move in the executive meeting?
choices: Interrupt and accuse the colleague
Say nothing and decide later
Calmly restate that you built the model
items.explanation: A factual restatement re-attaches your name without accusation.

items.prompt: Why not correct loudly in front of leadership?
choices: It can look like a fight
Leadership dislikes accurate information
A public correction would break company policy
items.explanation: A live conflict can overshadow who was actually right.

items.prompt: What is the next step after the meeting?
choices: A group message to the whole team
A private, specific, calm conversation
A louder repeat of the same correction in public
items.explanation: A private question gives the colleague a real chance to explain.

items.prompt: Why raise it privately before escalating?
choices: It hides your concern forever
It guarantees they will apologize to you
It lets them explain before you assume
items.explanation: Private first keeps the door open for a genuine explanation.

items.prompt: After a repeat, what starts to matter?
choices: A public vote on who is right in the room
A written record of dates and claims
Staying completely silent
items.explanation: Specific records support your own clarity and any later manager conversation.

items.prompt: Which of these is premature escalation?
choices: Going to your manager after one incident
Documenting dates and claims after a repeat
Holding a private conversation
items.explanation: Escalating before the colleague could explain burns credibility a real pattern would need.

items.prompt: What does "calibrated" mean here?
choices: As forceful as you can possibly be
As quiet as you can possibly manage
Matched to the evidence you have
items.explanation: Calibrated means neither silent nor a public trial.

items.prompt: With scapegoating, a calm correction attaches what to the facts?
choices: Your own name to someone else's work
The real decision and who made it
A new deadline for the whole project
items.explanation: The same principle applies: state the factual correction without accusation.

items.prompt: In the readout, the colleague presents your model as theirs. Which line is the most calibrated?
choices: "That is my work and you know it perfectly well, as everyone should see."
"Before we go any further, let the record show who actually did this."
"Glad it landed well; I built the model, happy to walk through it."
"Great presentation everyone, let us move on to the next item now."
items.explanation: It re-attaches your name factually and invites engagement, without accusing or conceding.
items.reference:
A response that scales with the evidence
🎤 In the room: restate your ownership, factually, without accusing
🤝 After: a private, specific, non-accusatory question
📝 If it repeats: document dates, claims and work products
📈 Then, if needed: bring it to your manager
Why: each step is proportional, so the answer you get actually works as evidence.
items.learnMore:
Calibrated means proportional

A calm restatement in the room, such as "happy to walk through the assumptions since I built the model," re-attaches your name without forcing anyone to take sides. A private question gives the colleague a real chance to explain. If the behavior repeats after that, a written record and a conversation with your manager become justified rather than premature.

Common mistake

Confronting publicly in the meeting, or staying silent and hoping it will not happen again.
items.reflection: Imagine this had been scapegoating instead of credit-stealing. What would the equivalent calm, factual correction sound like?

items.prompt: Why does restraint in the meeting matter for the private conversation that follows?
choices: It makes the colleague feel guilty enough to confess
It stops anyone from ever taking sides
It means you can skip the private conversation entirely
It keeps the later question open, so answers count
items.explanation: If you accused in the room, the private talk is a follow-up to a fight. Staying factual keeps the colleague's response informative.

items.prompt: After your private conversation, the colleague takes credit again the next month. What is the sound next step?
choices: Document dates, claims and work products, then consider your manager
Wait for a third instance before recording anything
Answer with a rumor so they feel a cost
Repeat the same private conversation again, word for word
items.explanation: A repeat after a conversation is strong evidence, so a specific record and a manager conversation are now warranted.

items.prompt: A colleague tells the room an outage came from a change you shipped, although the decision was made above you. Which immediate response mirrors the credit-stealing one?
choices: "That is a lie, and everyone here knows it perfectly well."
"I implemented it after the decision; I did not make it."
"I am happy to explain at the retro for whoever asks."
"It is my fault; I really should have pushed back."
items.explanation: Same principle, different fact: attach the decision to who made it, calmly, rather than accuse or accept blame you do not hold.
